text: Went to my first open source meetup today. Everyone there seemed to have merged PRs into big projects. Honestly it felt like real contributors are a different kind of person. I just sat at the back and didn't ask anything because I didn't want people to realise I've never contributed to anything.

Tried to read the contributing guide for a big Python library. Gave up after twenty minutes. There's so much setup and I don't even know which issue I'd pick. I keep thinking I need to be much better at coding before I'm allowed to touch a real project.

Applied to three internships this week. Two rejections already. I keep rewriting my resume but I don't have anything to show except college assignments. Maybe I need side projects that people can actually see.

Small win. I fixed a typo in the docs of a library I use and the maintainer merged it in an hour and said thanks. It's tiny but it's my first merged PR. Maybe contributing is less about being a genius and more about just starting with something small.

Started posting what I'm learning on LinkedIn. One post about my first merged PR got way more likes than I expected. A few people messaged me saying they also felt scared to contribute. Building in public feels uncomfortable but it's working.
Signed up for my first hackathon. I'm nervous because I don't know if I can build something in 24 hours. I keep imagining everyone else will be way more experienced and I'll just slow my team down.

Hackathon day one. Our team spent four hours arguing about the idea. Lesson: pick something small and start building early. The teams that scoped down are already demoing features. We're still setting up the repo.

Hackathon is over. We didn't win but we shipped a working demo. The judges cared way more about a clear demo than about how complex the code was. Next time I'll spend the last two hours only on the demo and the story.

Talked to a senior engineer at a meetup. She said nobody expects you to know everything on day one, and that she still googles basic things every day. That really stuck with me. Maybe the feeling of not knowing enough never fully goes away, and that's normal.

Got an interview for a backend internship. I was terrified but I prepared by explaining my side projects out loud. The interviewer asked more about my open source PRs than my grades. Showing real work is what counts.

Wrote a longer post about what I learned from my first hackathon. I keep noticing that writing about my work forces me to understand it better. Building in public is becoming a habit rather than something scary.

Joined a second hackathon, this time I pushed the team to scope down in the first hour. We had a demo ready by midnight and spent the morning polishing the pitch. Starting small really works. We got second place.

At the mentor table today I noticed the people who got furthest were the ones who asked where to start, not the ones who knew the most. I used to think asking questions made you look weak. Now I think it's the fastest way in.
Got the internship offer! Part of it was the projects I posted about publicly. My manager said she found my LinkedIn posts before my resume. Still feels unreal.

Starting to feel the imposter thing again at the new internship. Everyone talks in acronyms I don't know. But this time I'm writing them down and asking. It feels lighter than in May, I know the feeling passes if I keep showing up.
Made pasta from scratch for the first time with my flatmate. Way too much flour and the kitchen was a mess, but it was really fun and nice to do something completely away from screens.

Wikimedia hackathon. A mentor pointed me to a small bug in a citation tool and I fixed it in two hours. Skill wasn't the blocker at all. Not knowing where to start was. Small bugs really are the on-ramp into open source.

title: Mentor table notes
text: Notes from the mentor table: ask where to start, pick the smallest issue, and post about it afterwards. Three people asked me how I got my first PR merged. A few months ago I was the one sitting at the back too scared to ask.
